Saw a couple of people ask wonder how i do my motion designs and in general how to become better. Here are some tips that can help:

1. Download a motion design video you really love and then analyse it in whatever tool you use. Check how long it takes, try to match the easings, how are the staggering between. Recreate it. This way you also get a feel why some one does something

2. Learn about the fundamentals of motion design. Check the 12 motion principles by disney. Look for advanced motion courses etc

3. Find inspiration in other forms of motion. animation (anime, short films), dance videos, sword swinging videos, parkour videos, listen to music and get a feel of the rhythm etc

Motion is all about story telling and every good story needs overall pace, differing tempo, intonations, space to breath etc

And also be very honest with yourself about your practising routine - if you do a motion design every week or just a half hearted version each day you won't improve. Challenge yourself. Do what's hard.

Depending on how you look at it, it's both a blessing or a curse.

The consolidation of roles (due to AI) means that Designers are Developers now. And Developers are Designers. In particular on front-end.

In fact, I'd argue the top 20% of designers are now better front-end devs than 80% of all devs before.

And in the opposite direction, 20% of the top developers are now BETTER Designers than 80% of the Designers before, with their new combined skillset.

For some people this is a godsend gift, for others its their nightmare come true.

For me personally, I am split here. It's both for me, because I've never wanted the role of a engineer, but at the same time I enjoy it, because I'm quite effective.

But I need to remember myself: I get my satisfaction from being a Designer first and foremost, not engineering, regardless of how easy or difficult it is.

When I dream, I dream of designing, not implementing my designs. I don't dream about fixing bugs, chasing edge cases. I dream of problems that are solved on the emotional spectrum. All of which still would need someone competent and skillful to implement it.

Even with the consolidation of roles, I still believe that towards the top (both in reality and aspirationally), the specialization will hold true and keep existing.

Alright. I want you to read this.

Earlier today, I released a new component.

What you see is the finished result.

What you don’t see are the days of planning, research, testing, designing, simplifying, throwing ideas away, and trying again before I felt it was ready.

Within hours, it had been copied and ported to another framework by pointing an agent at my code.

Of course, it’s open source. They were allowed to do it.

And I’ve been around long enough, with multiple successful products, that I don’t care.

But what if this was someone’s first product?

What if they spent months building it, launched on Friday, and by Monday it had been cloned by agents, repackaged, and made free?

What happens when your second product is copied?

Your fifth?

Your tenth?

What happens when every new idea immediately becomes the next prompt?

What happens when your roadmap, your changelog, and your launch announcements become someone else input prompts?

What happens when models become good enough to copy bigger ideas?

What happens when “just execute better” stops being the answer?

What happens when “just build bigger” or “think wider” stops being enough?

What happens when both ideas and execution become cheap?

What happens when the creator pays the full cost of creativity but everyone else pays nothing to reproduce it?

What happens to creativity when AI makes copying effectively free?

What happens to the will to create when AI makes copying effectively free?

Look, copying is not new.

Copying at this speed, cost, and scale is.

People will tell you to think bigger.

But nobody starts "bigger".

Every one of us here started by making something small.

You keep going because, somewhere along the way, the work is rewarded.

Maybe people use it.

Maybe they pay for it.

Maybe they simply recognize the thought, effort, and care that went into it.

Copying once demanded effort.

You had to study the work and understand it to copy it.

That effort created appreciation for the person who made it.

Not anymore.

Creativity begins with small steps.

If we make those first steps feel pointless, we don’t just lose small products. 

We lose the people who might have gone on to build the big ones.

We are uniquely positioned here.

We get to use and experience this life-changing technology before almost everyone else.

How we use it will set the default everywhere else.

That default will spread to writing, design, music, research, and every other field where someone still has to take the first creative risk.

We can use AI to build great things.

Or we can use it to strip every new idea for parts.

We decide.

text:
if you're starting out w web design or feel like you've hit a plateau i recommend doing some of these or all:

- go on awwwards, take one site and rebuild it - you'll learn soo much
- learn the principles of design - spacing, visual hierarchy etc. many junior designers lack esp in these areas. a great design is great because the designer completely understood the fundamentals
- experiment - just go wild for once. don't think about the trends or what you should do, just have fun.
- go to museums, read fiction books, actively listen to a song/album - submerging yourself into art gets your mind into a creative introspective mood. very important to strengthen your connection to creativity
- go outside and talk a way without your phone - taking everything can relax your mind and open you up to new ideas
- ask other designers (more senior than you) for feedback - many times we need the perspective of an experienced designer to break our boxed in view. can also be any creative person 
- find a way to create art that isn't design - be it painting, writing poetry, dancing. these forms of art are much purer in it's purpose than design is. It allows you to connect w your creativity on a much deeper level and gives you new perspectives
- buy some books about graphic design - not the "how to" but w real life examples. get inspired by other designers.

These are just some ideas you can utilise in your process to level up your skill. It's very important to do things over and over again to hone your craft but sometimes we're at a dead end and can't seem to get better at what we do. No matter how hard we try. 

Hope these help. If you have any tips to go from junior to senior, from good to great, please feel free to write them down in the comments. 🙌🏻

a well designed button in product design isn't flashy. 

it's functional, scaleable and adaptable. 

think about components like an ecosystem within an ecosystem.

a button on its own is very simple. but many different elements have different requirements for a button. 

some need an icon on the left, some need an icon on the right. some need the button to stretch and some need it to be smaller.

working from a molecular level up is the key to a powerful and scalable design system. 

(also the devs will thank you when you create modular based components)

A lot of the posts that go viral here are just flashy. 

Look closer and you see a lot of issues.

The whole GO / Loud Ring section feels unpleasant to click and unbalanced. And the AM/PM has a gap on the right. 

That's just some issues but the overall thing is that just because you see a post like this go viral doesn't mean it's well executed.

Why do you think concepts and flashy things like this get hyped but features that are implemented in real products aren't?

It's because they're made to work effortlessly not to wow you. I guarantee if you'd use this component long enough you'd see many issues that aren't even visible in this screenshot.

So if you really want to learn good product design learn from existing applications. Use mobbin, download apps, demo test saas tools. 

You'll learn from real and highly skillful product designers.
